analysis.one_liner: Extends overtime, sick leave, contract, break, and anti-discrimination protections to domestic workers.
analysis.headline: S. 2112 drew 12 cosponsors but never got a hearing, markup, or vote; its only actions were introduction and referral to the Senate HELP Committee in July 2019, and it died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a federal bill of rights for the roughly 2.5 million nannies, home care aides, housekeepers, and cleaners who work in private homes. It would repeal the law that exempts live-in domestic workers from overtime pay, require written contracts covering pay and schedules, guarantee up to 56 hours a year of earned paid sick time, require meal and rest breaks, protect workers from retaliation, and extend federal anti-discrimination law to domestic workers. It would also boost federal Medicaid payments to states for the home care workforce.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic workers — disproportionately women, people of color, and immigrants — who today often work without written contracts, sick pay, or overtime. Their households and care recipients would also benefit from lower turnover and more stable care.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Fair Labor Standards Act exemption that has kept live-in domestic employees outside minimum wage and overtime requirements since 1938.

Households and agencies would have to give any domestic worker employed 8+ hours a week a signed written agreement covering pay rate, overtime, expected hours, on-call shifts, and termination policies, and could not require forced arbitration or non-disclosure agreements in it.

Domestic workers would earn one hour of paid sick time per 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours a year, usable for their own illness, a family member's care, or domestic violence and stalking situations.

The bill requires a 30-minute meal break after 5 hours and 10-minute rest breaks every 4 hours, paid at the regular rate, with exceptions when the safety of the person receiving care prevents a break.

Live-in workers who are fired would get at least 30 days of lodging or two weeks of severance pay, and employers could not penalize them for contacting clients directly rather than through a platform app.

The bill adds domestic workers to Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, giving them the same recourse as other workers against workplace discrimination and harassment, and makes threatening a worker's immigration status an unlawful form of retaliation.

The bill's own findings cite the bill sponsor's record: about 2.5 million domestic workers average roughly $11 an hour, fewer than 9 percent have payroll taxes paid for Social Security, and 91 percent of workers who had problems with working conditions did not complain because they feared losing their job.

analysis.who_pays: The households, care agencies, and on-demand care and cleaning platforms that employ domestic workers would bear new costs for overtime, sick pay, contracts, breaks, and severance. Some of that cost would be passed to families paying for care, and the federal government would fund the higher Medicaid match, a hotline, grants, and a new standards board.
analysis.who_pays_short: Care agencies, platforms, and hiring households

drawbacks.text: Compliance would fall heavily on individual households and small agencies that have never had to run payroll formalities; every hiring would require a signed multi-part written agreement, with a $5,000 penalty per worker for failing to provide one.
Firing a live-in worker would require 30 days of lodging or two weeks of severance, which could make households more hesitant to hire live-in help for an aging relative or a child.
The bill raises federal spending: it increases the Medicaid match for home care services and authorizes grants for a hotline, safety training, and outreach, with the cost left to appropriations.
Households paying out of pocket for care could face higher prices, and some informal arrangements — babysitting or cleaning paid in cash — could shift to the books or disappear.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a genuinely unprotected workforce: most federal labor laws still leave domestic workers out, and the conditions documented in its findings — poverty wages, no sick pay, fear of complaint — are severe. The main costs are real but concentrated on employers, particularly middle- and upper-income households and care companies, and part of that cost is the point: paying overtime and sick time that other workers already get. The paperwork burden on families hiring a single nanny is the strongest good-faith objection, though the bill exempts casual babysitters and family arrangements from its definition.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in July 2019 and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Kamala Harris introduced S. 2112 on July 15, 2019, joined by 12 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That referral was the bill's last action: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The households, home care agencies, and platforms that employ domestic workers are better off because the bill died: they kept the status quo with no new contract, sick pay, overtime, break, or severance obligations. The 2.5 million domestic workers the bill covered gained nothing, and no state of the law changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers of domestic workers kept the status quo

for.name: Kamala Harris
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act on July 15, 2019.

for.name: 12 Senate cosponsors (11 Democrats, 1 independent), including Kirsten Gillibrand, Cory Booker, Amy Klobuchar, Bernie Sanders, and Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it its full Senate support of 13 senators, all Democrats or independents.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chairman, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: After the bill was referred to the HELP Committee, the committee took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 senators behind the bill were Democrats or the independent Bernie Sanders, and no Republican cosponsored it; with Republicans chairing the HELP Committee and holding the Senate majority, the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and domestic staffing companies
industries.note: The bill would require written agreements, earned sick time, meal and rest breaks, and overtime for workers they currently schedule without these benefits, raising payroll costs. Their interest in avoiding those costs runs directly against the workers' wage and leave gains.

The bill would bar platforms from deducting wages or penalizing workers who communicate directly with clients instead of through the app, and would treat covered workers as entitled to contracts and sick pay. Platforms' flexible gig model depends on the informality the bill would end.

industries.industry: Households that hire live-in domestic help
industries.note: Firing a live-in worker would require 30 days of lodging or two weeks of severance, and hiring would require a formal written agreement. These families' savings depend on the current rules that exempt live-in workers from overtime and termination protections.

The bill would raise the federal Medicaid match for home care services and direct HHS to collect data on the aide workforce, channeling more federal money into home care pay and capacity. Higher pay for aides would be funded through this route, alongside their new labor rights.
